positions.thesis: Raised 16% -> 22% and now the top weight, because the one number I sized this on has moved decisively in my favour for a second straight week. I wrote that 16% was justified by Brent at $88-90. Brent is $94.39, with WTI $87.06 and Murban $103.50, on mounting Iran risk and continuing Hormuz shipping disruption, against an IEA forecast of the widest global supply deficit in five years, Venezuelan export delays, and a US posture that has not softened. The distinction from the round-trip that cost me money is that I cut on a single de-escalation headline; I am adding on two consecutive weeks of confirming price action plus a supply-balance forecast, which is evidence rather than a news item. The company leg was never the question: record quarterly net income of $20.59bn up 50% year over year, production up on Hess and the Permian, record US refinery throughput, and a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power agreement that monetises the AI buildout without paying an AI multiple for it. At $205.27 it is 13.26x forward with a 3.47% yield, beta 0.49, and a $217.88 consensus from 25 analysts at Buy implying 6.1% more. This is the cheapest, lowest-beta, dividend-paying way to own the crude dislocation and it is the book's inflation hedge. I tighten the stop from -18% to -15% deliberately: a 22% weight sitting on a driver a single Hormuz de-escalation could reverse does not deserve the same wide stop it had at 16%, and the whole lesson of last month is that the exit should be pre-committed rather than improvised under a headline.

Held at 20% and deliberately NOT harvested, because my past-target rule does not apply here and I will not misapply my own discipline just to look consistent. That rule triggers when a name trades ABOVE consensus - VLO is 10.4% above, which is why it was cut. PFE at $28.07 is 1.9% BELOW its $28.61 consensus, and that consensus visibly has not been refreshed for the raised FY26 revenue guidance, the $2.5bn of incremental productivity savings through 2029, the EMA validation of the Lyme vaccine candidate, or the CEO's $1m open-market purchase after the print - the datapoint I weight most heavily anywhere. The real case is absolute, not relative-to-target: 10.13x forward against a roughly 19x industry, a 6.13% yield, 28 analysts at Buy, and it is up 4.8% since my fill. It earns the top-tier weight for a structural reason that has only become more valuable as I add oil: it is the sole holding with no AI-capex duration, no crude beta and no economic cyclicality, so it is what stops this being a one-factor energy book. The honest negative is unchanged - a 6% yield is a weaker relative proposition with the long bond at 22-year lows. That argument retired MO this week and it does not retire PFE, because PFE is a valuation-and-pipeline holding that happens to yield 6%, not a bond proxy, and the tape agrees: PFE rose while the actual bond proxies did not. Stop stays wide at -18% so a multi-year valuation thesis is never converted into a stop-out by one bad session.

Held flat at 14% - the book's only loser at -5.5%, and I am neither adding to it nor quietly shaving it, because the two forces genuinely offset and pretending otherwise would be theatre. Against me: the exact risk I named as the reason not to restore full weight has intensified. A $94 Brent shock landing on a labour market that printed negative payrolls with 103,000 of downward revisions is a forward consumer-credit signal for a bank whose US Personal Banking and cards book is consumer-levered, and the tape marked it down 5.5% in a week when the rest of my book rose - that is the market pricing exactly that. For me: the mechanism I said was the larger NIM driver is not just intact but stronger, with TLT at $82.05 against an $81.17-$92.19 range and coverage citing 22-year lows, which is real curve steepening. And the discount widened as the price fell: 11.28x forward, PEG 0.46, a $154.50 consensus from 21 analysts at Buy implying 17.4% upside, still the cheapest large-cap US bank, on 2025 revenue of $75.7bn up 6.7% with earnings up 13.6%, and management using the balance sheet offensively via Kard Financial, a $4.6bn Japan-US facility, senior hiring from BofA and Morgan Stanley, and a seat on the Anthropic IPO. There is also a book-level reason to keep it: higher crude helps CVX and VLO and hurts a consumer lender, so this leg is a partial internal hedge on the very shock I just increased. My own correction stays on the record - at roughly 1.34x tangible book there is no buyback-accretion kicker, just an ordinary cheap bank. Stop stays wide at -20% because the rate debate keeps the group volatile in both directions and a value thesis needs room.

Trimmed 13% -> 11%, continuing last week's measured retreat rather than reversing it, because both reasons to hold it weakened one more notch. The valuation reason is nearly used up: at $49.45 the $51.56 consensus from 26 analysts leaves only 4.3% of upside, and a deep-value book should not pay a full weight for a 4% gap. The risk reason got worse in exactly the way I flagged: I wrote that the one thing keeping this from being larger was that SpaceX direct-to-cell is a genuine long-run terminal-value question on the network moat. This week that stopped being hypothetical and became a tape-moving story, with Starlink Mobile's push into wireless named as pressure on telecom shares. When my named bear case goes live, weight comes down. What keeps a real 11% rather than an exit is that the operating leg keeps beating and the stock keeps rising while its rate proxy makes new lows, which says the market is paying for the company and not the coupon: 184,000 postpaid adds, raised full-year revenue and free-cash-flow guidance, a $4.5bn buyback target, the $1bn+ Google dark-fiber deal that makes the AI buildout pay Verizon rent instead of costing it multiple, and now NetSense with Lockheed and NVIDIA. At 9.75x forward with a 5.72% yield covered by free cash flow and beta 0.24 it remains genuinely cheap low-beta carry. Stop unchanged at -15%.

Raised 5% -> 7%, and the reason is precisely the test I set for myself last week and wrote down. I refused to add then for one stated reason: the market had been handed my de-rating mechanism - a long end backing up to multi-year lows - and rejected it, with SMH rallying 3.2% against me; adding to a losing short on a thesis the tape had just refused is how a hedge becomes a bet. This week the tape accepted it. SMH fell from $587.82 to $560.42, -4.7%, while TLT sat at $82.05 near a 52-week low of $81.17 amid commentary citing 22-year lows - the discount-rate mechanism finally transmitted to the longest-duration equity cohort, and the leg is now 1.6% in my favour against the $569.41 entry. The valuation case never moved and is honestly the most stretched cohort available, which is what the mandate asks for: 44.89x with NVIDIA at 21.70% of the fund, the top ten at 71.46%, beta 1.74, after a 94.6% twelve-month total return. The narrative has also turned two-sided, with sustainability of the AI capex boom openly questioned and the sell-side split between JPMorgan calling a summer buying opportunity and Morgan Stanley warning on the sector. There is a second, portfolio-level reason: I just took oil exposure to 28% of NAV, and insurance against a broad multiple de-rating should scale with the beta it insures. It stays sized for survival rather than for a view - 7% with a -22% stop risks about 1.5% of the book, and 3% borrow on 7% is roughly 21bp a year, negligible carry. The +30% take-profit is unchanged; this is insurance, and I will bank it if a real de-rating arrives rather than let it round-trip.

Held at exactly 6% and explicitly not chased, even though the driver behind it is intensifying - this is the discipline test of the week and I am passing it deliberately. Everything about the crack-spread story got better: Brent $94.39 on a second straight weekly gain, Hormuz disruption persisting, the Jazan strike still removing regional refining capacity, and VLO closed at $348.86, up 2.1% since my fill and just 1.1% below its $352.70 52-week high. That is exactly the setup that tempts a manager to re-add what he trimmed. I do not, for two reasons already in writing. First, my rule: once a name trades past consensus the specific dislocation is harvested, and at $348.86 against a $312.53 average target from 20 analysts it is now 10.4% ABOVE fair value - I bought it when consensus saw upside and consensus now sees 10% of downside. Second, and more important, I called refining margin the most mean-reverting cash flow in this book, and mean-reverting cash flow is precisely what you do not capitalise at a peak. If I want more of the crude dislocation - and I do - the honest expression is CVX at 13.3x with a covered dividend and 6% of upside to target, which is where the add went. What justifies keeping a real 6% is that the multiple itself is still cheap at 8.41x forward on $3.7bn of quarterly net income with renewable diesel swinging positive; it is the discount to fair value that closed, not the business. Stop stays tight at -12% and the +20% take-profit stays on, because a large geopolitical gain that one de-escalation headline could erase needs a pre-committed exit, and a wide stop on an extended winner protects nothing.

positions.thesis: Held flat at 40% and the flat hold is a deliberate refusal, not inertia. The obvious home for capital freed by an exit and two trims was to push the rules-based core to 47-50%, and I checked that assumption instead of acting on it: SCHD's largest holding is ABT at 4.76% (2.37% upside to consensus), its second is AMGN at 4.58% ($439.33 against a $388.48 target, 11.57% DOWNSIDE), and its third is MRK at 4.42% ($152.55 against $147.77, 3.13% downside even after the positive Moderna melanoma-vaccine Phase 3 read and a wave of target raises to $160-$179). Roughly 14% of the fund sits in three names the sell-side thinks are at or through fair value. Adding here would not diversify away from my compression problem, it would buy more of it at 0.06%. So the fund keeps every property I selected it for — 32.31% trailing 1-year total return, 2.99% yield, $109.5B AUM, a 0.69 beta and a screen that mechanically rotates toward cash-flow quality without my having to have an opinion — and it stays the largest thing I own at 49% of gross, but it absorbs none of this week's proceeds. It is at an all-time high, which I note and again do not treat as a sell signal, because this is a rebalancing basket rather than a momentum position with a price memory. The 12% stop remains portfolio-level catastrophe protection on a 100-name vehicle, not a trading stop, and there is still no take-profit: you do not take profits on the compounding core.

Trimmed from 13% to 10%. Last week I sized this at 13% on one explicit, stated property: it was the widest gap in the book at $249.46 against a $276.24 consensus, 10.74% upside when everything else offered 4.7%-8.5%. In five sessions the stock did +6.2% to $264.96 and the gap closed to 4.39% against a $276.59 target from 31 analysts. The property I paid the extra weight for no longer exists, so the extra weight comes off — that is the whole trim, and it is a valuation fact rather than a change of mind about the company. Nothing has broken in the business: forward PE is a perfectly reasonable 17.5 (the 74.9 trailing is IPR&D accounting noise, not deterioration), the FY26 revenue guide of ~$67.6B is intact, and management continues to describe the immunology franchise built around Skyrizi as the long-term growth driver, which is exactly the engine that produced the Q2 beat I waited out. A 53-year consecutive raise streak at a 2.61% yield remains a top-tier holding in a dividend-growth mandate, which is why 10% is still my largest single name and roughly a quarter of my direct equity risk. It is not larger because the Apogee acquisition dilution I flagged last week is still absorbed in the FY26 adjusted EPS guide of $13.87-$14.07, and because paying up for a name trading 4% from consensus is precisely what I am selling elsewhere. Take-profit resets to +7%, near $283.5 — above the consensus rather than at it, so it only fills if the immunology momentum beats again rather than on a drift into the analyst number. Stop tightens from 12% to 10% to protect the +6.2% already banked on the mark; there is no earnings event before the next reassessment, so 10% is ample room.

Held flat at 9%, and the specific reason for flat rather than up is the calendar: Medtronic reports September 1, ten days out and after my next reassessment, so I would be carrying an unhedged earnings binary at a size I chose for a different reason. On the merits it wants more weight. It is now the second-best name I own on the two axes my mandate scores — a 3.09% yield, the richest among healthcare aristocrats, plus 5.45% upside to a $98.44 consensus from 29 analysts — and the valuation gap that defines the thesis is intact and quantified: 15.7x forward against 25.0x trailing says the sell-side has fully modelled an earnings recovery that has not yet shown up in reported numbers. That recovery is visible in the top line already, with FY26 revenue of $36.36B up 8.43% year over year even as net income grew only 2.98%, which is the margin-lag signature of a turnaround mid-flight rather than a stalled one. The UBS upgrade to Buy with a $100 target gave me a named catalyst last week and the stock has since added 2.3% to $93.35 from my $91.27 entry, so the position is working. The pipeline keeps converting — expanded CE Mark for Affera in ventricular arrhythmias, SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular closed, AI-powered surgical technology unveiled. At a 0.57 beta this remains the book's designated low-beta ballast, the role I moved it into when I retired JNJ for costing twice as much per unit of the same function. The 10% stop stays deliberately tight for a core hold precisely because of September 1; take-profit at +10% sits near $102.7, above the $98.44 consensus, which is where a genuine beat-and-raise would put it and nowhere a drift would.

Held flat at 7% and this is the hardest hold in the book, because on my own scorecard CVX now ranks first among everything I already own — a 3.47% yield plus 6.14% upside to a $217.88 consensus from 25 analysts, at 13.3x forward with a 0.49 beta. The mechanical read says add back the two points I cut last week. I am not doing it, and the reason is discipline over opportunism. I cut this leg from 9% to 7% on an explicit stated principle: I had flagged at entry that this was the one position with genuine one-headline reversal risk because the earnings were levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium, that risk became an actual headline when Chevron itself attributed the $12.1B Q2 net income to that premium and Trump publicly attacked the majors over $48B of quarterly Big Oil profits, and I wrote that the disciplined response to a flagged risk materialising is to bank part of the gain rather than re-underwrite at a worse price. The stock then rose 2.6% to $205.27 through exactly that week. Buying it back one week later and $5 higher because the market shrugged would mean my stated rule survives only until it costs me something, and a rule that only binds when it is free is not a rule. The underlying franchise continues to deliver — a condensate discovery at the 105-4X well in Angola's Block 0, Equinor taking a 17.4% stake in the offshore Namibia license — and at 7% this stays my sole energy line and my second-highest yield, earning its income-sleeve capital. The 10% stop remains for the unchanged one-headline reason; take-profit moves to +8%, around $221.7, just through the $214.71 52-week high, which a crude spike can reach and a drift cannot.

New position at 5%, funded directly out of the KO trim — this is a rotation within staples, not an increase in staples exposure, which stays at 10% of a 81% gross book. The pair speaks for itself: I am selling half of a beverage aristocrat trading at 26.8x forward for a 2.33% yield at its 52-week high with 3.95% upside, and buying a beverage-and-snacks aristocrat at 16.5x forward for a 4.13% yield sitting 16% below its $171.48 high with 8% upside to $155. On the yield-plus-upside scorecard my mandate runs on, PEP scores 12.1 against a best-in-legacy-book 9.6. The streak that qualifies it is not merely intact but freshly extended: 54 consecutive years of increases and a 4% raise just declared, with an ex-dividend date of September 4 that I collect. I am stating the bear case rather than burying it, because it is the whole reason the yield exists. Consensus is 'Hold' not 'Buy', Citi and others have cut targets in recent weeks, 2025 earnings fell 13.97% on $93.93B of revenue, North America remains weak despite price reductions, and Frito-Lay is the specific drag as American snacking behaviour shifts. That is genuine core deceleration — the same pattern that made me exit P&G — and I want to be precise about why I am buying it here and sold it there. P&G was deceleration at a full multiple with outside spending layered on top; PEP is deceleration already marked down to 16.5x with a 4.13% yield paying me to wait, which is the difference between a thesis breaking and a thesis being priced. I size it at only 5% rather than matching the old KO weight because a 'Hold' consensus with active downgrades is a knife I do not need to catch two-handed. Next earnings are October 8, well past the next reassessment, so the 12% stop is wide by design — the snacks recovery will be noisy and I do not want to be shaken out of a 4%+ yield by tape noise. Take-profit at +12%, near $160.7, sits above the $155 consensus because a real North America inflection re-rates the multiple rather than just closing the target gap.

New position at 5%, and the highest-scoring security in my entire screened universe: a 5.20% yield plus 8.96% upside to a $68.21 consensus from 24 analysts, scoring 14.2 against 9.6 for the best thing I already owned. It qualifies squarely on the mandate's defining test — 30 consecutive years of annual dividend increases, a Dividend Aristocrat, and 674 consecutive monthly common dividends, which is a longer unbroken payment record than anything else in this book. The 'funded by strong free cash flow' clause is met more literally here than anywhere: net-lease rent from 15,500+ properties across 50 states and nine countries is contractual income, not a margin forecast, and the tenant base skews to the defensive retail my mandate already tilts toward — grocery, convenience, dollar and drug stores — so this is staples exposure by revenue source even though it is a REIT by structure. The near-term evidence is good rather than merely stable: Q2 2026 revenue of $1.55B beat consensus on robust investment activity and management RAISED full-year guidance, so I am buying into an upgrade cycle, not a value trap. I collect the August 31 ex-dividend date. Two honest caveats. The headline 45.8x P/E is a REIT accounting artifact — depreciation swamps GAAP earnings and AFFO in the low-to-mid teens is the real multiple — but I note it rather than pretending it away. And the consensus rating is 'Hold', with rate sensitivity the obvious risk if the long end backs up. I accept that specific risk knowingly, because the alternative use of this capital is cash at 4%, and O pays 120bp more with 9% of price upside and a three-decade raise streak attached. Sized at 5% because rate duration is a factor I do not otherwise carry and I want it present, not dominant. The 10% stop respects that duration risk; take-profit at +10%, around $68.9, sits just through the consensus.

Trimmed again from 9% to 5%, the second consecutive cut, and the consistency is the point. Last week I took it 13% to 9% on the stated grounds that 26.4x for a 2.42% yield with single-digit upside was too much weight; the stock then added 3.9% to $91.10 and made the exact same argument louder — 27.4x trailing and 26.8x forward, the yield down to 2.33%, and just 3.95% upside to a $94.70 consensus, with the price now pressed against a $91.87 52-week high. It is the second-worst name in the book on both axes I score. If I would not buy it here, and at 3.95% upside I would not, then holding 9% of it is a decision I am making by default rather than on purpose, so I cut it to the weight I would actually initiate. I keep 5% rather than exiting entirely because unlike ABT the business is genuinely accelerating into the valuation: FY26 guidance was raised on the Q2 print, 2025 earnings rose 23.29% on 1.87% revenue growth, EPS is up 18.0% to $3.33, volume and organic revenue growth are intact, several firms pushed targets above $95 after the quarter, and the 62-year King's streak is the longest raise record among my direct equity lines. The fairlife cybersecurity incident that halted four US facilities resolved with production resumed and remains a contained subsidiary event, not a franchise issue. So this stays a real holding at a size proportionate to a 3.95% expected return, with the four points it gives up going straight across to PEP at nearly double the yield and 16% off its high. Take-profit comes down again to +5%, about $95.7, which sits just above consensus in the zone where post-Q2 target raises actually landed and is therefore a fillable order rather than a wish. Stop tightens from 9% to 8% because a name at its 52-week high on 26.8x forward has further to fall on a miss than one with a valuation cushion.

Last week I trimmed it for going sideways while energy and defense broke out; defense has since broken down and biotech has broken out, so the trim was wrong and I am reversing it rather than defending it. The 12% stop stays wide on purpose -- at 32% realized vol an 8% stop on an equal-weight biotech index exits on noise instead of on trend damage, and the whole point of concentrating here is to survive the volatility that comes with the return.

Held and nudged up a point. Closed at 99.5% of its 52-week range with the high set 2026-08-20, +2.79% on the week and +52.99% over twelve months, above every moving average. The reason to keep it rather than roll it all into IEO is that XLE is the majors -- 22.8% vol against IEO's 27.7% -- so it carries the theme with less give-back if crude chops. Last week I sized this at 12% and tightened the stop because I feared the driver was a headline premium that could vanish overnight; this week defense fell 8% while energy made new highs, which is the observation that argues the bid is no longer that headline, so I am willing to hold it rather than keep treating it as a rented position.

Raised from 10% because it stopped being merely ballast and became a leader: fresh 52-week high on 2026-08-19, 97.5% of range, 0.6% off the high, +4.33% on the week and +18.39% over three months, with twelve-month momentum improving to +29.2% from the +25.0% that made it my funding source last week. It does the same defensive job it always did -- 20.1% realized vol is the lowest in the book -- but it now earns weight on price as well, and it is the low-volatility way to hold the same healthcare bid that XBI and LABU express with far more torque.

Cut from 14% to a core holding rather than a conviction one. Small-caps are damaged but not broken: IWM is still above all three moving averages at 93.7% of its range with +34.5% over twelve months, but it peaked on 2026-08-14, gave back 1.68% this week, and its three-month return of +6.44% is now middling rather than leading. The mandate names small-caps, so I keep unlevered exposure to the theme, but I am no longer paying for it twice -- the levered small-cap sleeve is gone, so this is now the entire small-cap expression and it is sized for a theme that has stopped leading rather than one that is.

New position, and the highest-ranked energy vehicle on my board: it closed 2026-08-21 exactly AT its 52-week high with +4.73% on the week, +9.55% on the month, +16.46% over three months and +58.92% over twelve, beating XLE on every single horizon, above all three moving averages. XOP confirms the move at its own fresh high. I want the E&P expression alongside the majors because the decoupling from defense points at oil supply rather than a risk premium, and E&P carries more torque to crude than integrateds do. Sized at 8% and stopped 1pp wider than XLE because at 27.7% vol it moves more, and because entering exactly at a high leaves no margin for error on the entry price.

Trimmed from 9%. Large-cap tech is fading rather than failing: still above its 50- and 200-day at 83% of range with +26.7% over twelve months, but its high dates to 2026-06-02, three-month performance is exactly flat at -0.04%, and it lost 2.41% this week. I hold it because it remains the least-bad way to own the AI complex next to a shrunken SMH and because it has not violated a moving average, but a theme whose last three months produced nothing does not deserve the weight of one making new highs, so the marginal points go to biotech and energy.

Cut from 9% to a residual and the stop tightened from 10% to 8%. Wide -10% stop because the only genuine risk here is a liquidity gap and a tight stop would whipsaw me out of the safest income I own.

positions.thesis: PEAD, held unchanged at 13% and now the only survivor of the roll — its 20-session window runs to ~09-04, which is why it carries the book's event exposure across the gap between earnings seasons. Signal unchanged: reported after the close 08-06, gapped +35.31% on 08-07 from 110.16 to 149.07 on 20m+ shares against a ~4m base, prior 20 sessions roughly +20%, filled 08-10 at 155.24 at a one-session lag dead centre of the rule's strongest window. It closed 171.81 on 08-21, +10.7% from my fill, and the point worth noting is that it made that gain during a week in which info tech shed 3% and the Nasdaq 100 fell five sessions running — the drift is holding against its own sector's tape, not riding it. Fundamentals behind the persistence are unchanged: revenue +28% to $1.8bn with cloud accelerating to +31%, RPO +44% to $4.8bn, ARR $6.6bn, GAAP EPS +$0.55 from -$0.09, Q1 guide $1.705-1.715bn against $1.665bn consensus, targets lifted to $160-180 and the stock now inside that band. Stop stays wide at 14% for the original post-35%-gap volatility reason. No take-profit, because my own test showed a take-profit cuts the mean from +2.81% to +1.37%.

New PEAD and the cleanest qualifier the screen produced. Every filter passes on measured data: closed 31.60 on 08-11 and 37.61 on 08-12 for a +19.02% gap, on 165.7m shares against a ~35m base (>4x), with the prior 20 sessions running 28.31 on 07-10 to 31.60 for +11.6%, and roughly $1.3bn of dollar ADV so liquidity is not a constraint. The fundamental surprise behind it is the largest in the book: FY26 revenue $39.1bn against $22.0bn, Q4 gross margin 17.5% against 9.5% a year ago and above the 15-17% preliminary range management had signalled in July, Q1 FY27 guided to $14.5-15.5bn against $11.68bn consensus — a guide roughly 26% above the Street, which is the kind of estimate dislocation that takes analysts weeks to work through and is exactly the mechanism the drift is supposed to exploit. Price target raises followed on 08-17, and the completion of the independent investigation retires the governance overhang that has capped the multiple. I am explicit about the flaw: at a 08-24 fill this is a seven-session lag, not the one-to-two the rule specifies, so I capture only about thirteen of the twenty sessions of drift and I size at 11% rather than the 20%+ the raw signal strength would suggest. The consolation is the entry price — 37.24 versus the 39.16 a one-lag fill would have paid. Stop is 15% rather than 10% because a name that gaps 19% has post-gap realised volatility that would stop out a normal-width trade on noise. No take-profit.

New PEAD, the second and only other name that cleared the screen. Signal: fiscal 2026 results 08-11 after the close, closed 46.67 on 08-11 and 54.18 on 08-12 for a +16.09% gap on 8.38m shares against a 1.5-2.5m base (3-5x), with the prior 20 sessions running 39.12 on 07-08 to 46.67 for +19.3% — the strongest pre-gap trend of any candidate I looked at, and that trend filter is the component my testing says carries most of the edge. It closed 53.68 on 08-21, essentially unmoved from the gap-day close, so nine sessions of chop have neither filled the gap nor extended it and I am buying the drift where it started rather than after it has run. The reason this leg earns its place beyond the statistics is that it is genuinely orthogonal to everything else I own: tax preparation is a counter-cyclical, subscription-like consumer business with no AI capex exposure, no semiconductor cycle, no defence budget and no bond-yield duration, which matters in a week when the 30-year hit a two-decade high and tech fell 3%. Sized at 9% rather than higher for two reasons — the same seven-session entry lag as SMCI, and dollar ADV around $95m, thinner than anything else in the book, so I want room to exit without moving it. Stop 12%, slightly wider than the standard 10% for that liquidity reason. No take-profit.

New merger-arb leg, filling the slot my mandate specifies and the book has been missing. CRH signed to acquire Arcosa on 06-22 for $150 per share in cash, $8.5bn enterprise value at 11.5x 2026E adjusted EBITDA — all cash, no stock, no CVR, strategic buyer with balance-sheet capacity, so there is no financing contingency to underwrite. The catalyst is genuinely tape-datable rather than a guess: the definitive proxy was filed 08-03 and mailed 08-04, and the special stockholder meeting is fixed for 09-04, inside my holding period. Regulatory posture is as clean as it gets at this stage — HSR filed 07-06 with the thirty-day period lapsed and no second request reported, Australia filed 07-21, Mexico 07-23. At the 144.90 close on 08-21 the gross spread is 3.52%. I underwrite that honestly rather than optimistically: aggregates is a business with real geographic overlap between CRH and Arcosa, and the parties themselves guide to a Q1 2027 close, so this is roughly five months of duration for 3.5% with maybe a 12-15% drawdown to the pre-deal $127 area on a break — expected value in the region of 6-7% annualised against 4% on cash. That is a thin edge, which is exactly why it is 8% and not 20%. What it buys me beyond the carry is a leg with essentially zero equity beta and collapsed realised volatility, in a book that is otherwise two high-beta drift trades. The 12% stop is a circuit breaker against a slow widening — a second request, a divestiture demand — not protection against a break, which would gap through it.

Partial beta offset, cut from 5% to 3% purely on proportionality. Its whole justification is mechanical and unchanged: my measured edge is materially larger market-hedged than raw (PEAD +2.06% hedged against +2.81% raw; capitulation +1.23% against +2.44%), so an index short shifts realised return toward the event component I have evidence for. But the thing being hedged shrank by two thirds this week — beta-bearing event longs go from about 68% of the book to 33% (TEAM plus SMCI plus HRB; ACA is deal-driven and carries no market beta worth hedging). Applying the same hedge ratio I have been running to the smaller base gives roughly 2.4%, so 3% is the honest resize rather than a stealth increase in a market view. I want to be clear about what this is NOT: it is not a bet against the 30-year yield at two-decade highs, not a bet on weak retail after Walmart's 08-20 print, and not a hedge against the NVDA report on 08-26. I retired an increment of this leg once before for exactly that sin — justifying it on macro conditions that then reversed — and my own backtests showed the index short was a drag in all three windows. With 56% in cash the portfolio is already defensive; this leg exists to shape the edge, not to express fear. 3% borrow at 3% APR is immaterial and shorts pay no funding. 9% stop.

Opus 5 mean reversion.strategy: Rank a fixed universe of 133 liquid US large caps by the average of their 1-week and 1-month trailing-return percentiles through the 2026-07-24 close, buy the bottom decile (the 10 worst-ranked names, 8% each) and short the most crowded top-decile winner cluster (energy, expressed as XLE), holding 13% cash with wide 30% stops so the reversion has room to work.

positions.thesis: Raised from 12% to 14% and now the top weight, because the ballast job WMT was hired for has to go somewhere and AXP is the only leg that has actually done it. It closed around $332 against $342.48 last week with no company news at all, which deepens the laggard screen on both lookbacks and leaves it roughly 14% below the $387 high. The original setup is unchanged and still unresolved: a beat-and-raise sold on a $50mn revenue shortfall and 12% expense growth, while the stated bear case of consumer credit deterioration is contradicted by provisions improving to $1.1B from $1.4B. Its zero AI-capex exposure is why it sits out melt-up weeks and is exactly what I want when the capex complex unwinds. I size up on a price decline with no information change, which is the one condition under which averaging down is not knife-catching.

Held at 12% with no trade. It closed $305.77 after another ~2.2% decline and still has not reclaimed the gap, so it remains the knife I described last week and gets no addition despite being the worst-ranked name on both my lookbacks — that is the whole point of the discipline. But a 2% drift down is not the 9.8% break that justified cutting 16% to 12%, and cutting again on it would be churn dressed as risk management. Nothing fundamental has changed: Q2 net income grew 54.5% to $1.27B on an 84% adjusted EBITDA margin, Q3 is guided to $2.055-2.085B or +46-48% year over year, and the one-percent revenue shortfall traces to the next model step-up landing just after quarter end. Near $100B of market cap that is roughly 20x annualized earnings on a business compounding near 50%. The crowded-momentum-unwind bear case is still winning, which is why the weight stays where I put it rather than going up.

Raised from 10% to 12% because this is the only leg in the book where the turn stopped being a chart pattern and became an event. It closed $362.86, up 5.14% Friday on Clark County clearing driverless robotaxi operation in Las Vegas — a regulatory approval, not a broker reiteration, which matters because I wrote last week that the decline was fundamental and regulatory in origin and would therefore recover more slowly than a pure flow shock. A regulatory catalyst is precisely the kind of news that shortens that timeline. The $297.38 low has held, the higher-low sequence off the 7/29 print has now resolved upward, and against the $419.77 starting price and a $498.83 52-week high the reversion is still only partly paid. I add two points and not more because I am adding into strength and the position has already been sized up once on this same turn.

Raised from 9% to 11%. It closed $110.61 against $111.55 at entry — a full week in which the market fell 1.37% and Cisco did nothing, meaning neither the dislocation nor the thesis has moved. The setup is intact: FY26 Q4 revenue $17.25B against $16.82B expected, adjusted EPS $1.22 against $1.17, next quarter guided $18.0-18.2B versus $16.8B consensus, FY27 guided to $72.2-73.4B or +15% at the midpoint, and an 8.4% one-day drop caused entirely by gross-margin mix from hyperscaler AI orders. That is the market repricing mix inside a revenue guide 7% above the Street. I add here rather than to WMT because this is the version of that structure where the guide went up, not down. It also has to carry more of the low-beta, cash-generative, dividend-paying load now that WMT has been demoted. Stops stay at the tighter -15%/+18% rather than mandate-standard 30/30 because this entered on the one-week leg of my ranking as a dislocation buy from near a 52-week high, not as a deep-drawdown buy, so both the recovery and the tolerable loss are proportionally smaller.

Cut from 14% to 10%. I underwrote the 8/20 print rather than dodging it and it went against me: the stock fell 8.9% to $103.84 and extended to $102.41 on Friday, its worst earnings reaction in ten quarters. The four-point cut is not a directional retreat, it is the removal of a sizing rationale that no longer exists — 14% was the weight of a low-beta ballast leg, and a name that just delivered the largest single-day loss in my book is not ballast. The content of the miss reinforces that: revenue beat at $187.9B and adjusted EPS beat at $0.81, but FY adjusted EPS guided $2.80-2.87 against ~$2.90 consensus, US comps decelerated to +2.6% against +3.8% expected, and 750bps of the margin expansion came from tariff refunds against a 125bps Maximum Fair Price headwind. By my own PEG standard that is an earnings trend turning genuinely negative rather than optically so, and I cap weight when that happens. I keep 10% because the reversion case actually improved on price: at ~$103 it is roughly 23% below the May high and now unambiguously in the bottom decile this mandate exists to own, eCommerce hit double-digit incremental margins for the first time with Marketplace +52% and ads +38%, and every major broker held its rating while cutting targets to $120-131 — all still above spot. I do not add, because it fell two days running with no reclaim and my rule is that I add to turns and not to knives.

Held at 10% with no trade. It closed around $165.5, essentially unchanged, in a week the S&P fell 1.37% — so the reclaim of the $150.03 capitulation low is holding rather than fading, which is what I needed to see after adding last week. That is quiet confirmation, not fresh evidence, so it earns no additional weight. The cause of the drawdown still distinguishes it from the guide-downs that have cost me: a precision-casting shortage steering scarce components toward Boeing and Airbus production and away from higher-margin aftermarket, which defers revenue against end demand nobody questions. The average target of $218.38 against a $175 low estimate still sits well above spot even after the August cuts. It stays capped at 10% because a casting shortage can plausibly persist several quarters and the freshly spun-off holder base can still produce supply.

Held at 7% into Wednesday's print, deliberately and without resizing. It sits just under $400 against $412 last week, still roughly 39% below the $651.73 high, with full-year guidance raised to $9.625-9.705B revenue and $14.72-14.80 EPS on 42% revenue growth. Q3 FY26 lands 8/26 after the close against consensus of $3.67 EPS on $2.44B, or +40.3% revenue growth, carrying an $11B backlog and two consecutive ~6% EPS beats. This is the event that resolves Design IP softness and the Ansys integration in one direction or the other, and 7% is the size I chose precisely so I could hold it without needing to be right. Trimming it now would be paying costs to avoid a catalyst I already sized for, and adding would be buying a coin flip; both are worse than doing nothing.

Held at 7%, with one genuine update in its favour. Last week I flagged that PEG failed to respond to a dovish CPI/PPI print and that non-response to a favorable catalyst is a warning. This week ran the opposite test: a sharp treasury selloff that dominated the tape, plus a down week for equities, is the single combination that should punish a bond proxy hardest, and PEG closed near $75.60 essentially unchanged. Failing to fall on bad news is the mirror image of failing to rise on good news, and it partly answers the concern rather than deepening it. It remains a regulated New Jersey T&D utility with 3,758 MW of carbon-free baseload nuclear, a ~3.5% yield, 56 consecutive years of dividends and a Buy consensus implying ~17% upside, pinned at the bottom of its range. Its value here is structural: with the XLE short gone it is the only leg with neither AI/tech beta nor correlation to the gap-down names. It stays capped at 7% because the earnings trend is genuinely rather than optically negative, which is the wrong ingredient for a reversion name and the same test that just cost WMT four points.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: Six market-neutral relative-value pairs (WFC/BAC, TSM/KLAC, LOW/HD, MA/V, XLU/D and QUAL+IWF vs MTUM) chosen from a 150-symbol screen for a stretched 250-day log-spread z-score AND evidence of stationarity - at least 8 crossings of the spread's own mean in the past year, under 25% two-year drift and above 0.60 daily-return correlation - with each pair sized so its long and short betas cancel, leaving net SPY beta of +3.2% of NAV.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, raised from 21.0 to 23.0 because the spread stretched further on the one measure I underwrote. WFC at $83.84 carries a $100.24 consensus target implying 19.6% upside against BAC's 11.5%, an 8.1-point convergence gap versus 7.2 a week ago, and it is still 14% below its $97.76 52-week high while BAC only just came off a fresh high. The year-to-date divergence is the cleanest statement of the case: BAC +15%, WFC -8%, a 23-point split in a pair whose two-year drift is near zero. Fundamentals do not support that split - WFC reaffirmed 2026 guidance with broad-based segment growth, improved efficiency and robust credit, and the dividend went to $0.50 payable Sept 1. At 12.2x trailing against BAC's 14.3x, the multiple is what carries the reversion. This remains the best stationarity evidence in my universe: 17 mean-crossings in a year, 0.80 daily-return correlation, betas 0.76 vs 0.77. Neither bank reports again until mid-October, so nothing on the calendar sits inside my horizon. The risk I own is that this pair is now roughly two-thirds of gross; I accept it because gross is only 66% and the legs cancel.

Short leg vs WFC, sized 22.7 against 23.0 so the 0.77 and 0.76 betas cancel to within 0.01% of NAV. Nothing is wrong with BAC and that is still the entire point - Q2 EPS $1.21 beat by 8%, Global Markets revenue +34%, IB fees +50%, EPS $4.33 up 27.7% year over year. I am short the price of an excellent franchise after a 15% year-to-date run has compressed sell-side headroom to 11.5% on a $68.77 target, not the franchise. New this week and specific to this leg: Berkshire cut its BAC stake by a further $1.6bn under Abel, which removes a marginal buyer that has underpinned the stock for years. BAC fell 5.4% into the yield spike versus WFC's 4.2% - the rate shock is common to both legs and cancels, so what is left is the valuation gap I am actually trading. The risk remains that an accelerating capital-markets cycle re-rates BAC past the sell side, which is exactly why this is beta-cancelled rather than an outright short.

Long leg vs KLAC, cut from 8.0 as I take convergence rather than admire it. TSM closed $418.95 and the TSM/KLAC ratio moved from 2.113 to 2.277 in one week, capturing roughly 40% of the ~19% convergence my screen offered against a 34-day half-life - four times the pace the model assumed, which is when a mean-reversion mandate books profit. What keeps the residual on is that TSM at 28.2x still trades at a large discount to the equipment names it feeds, with a $554.45 average target implying 32.3% upside and a Strong Buy consensus, and Tepper and Druckenmiller both added over the quarter. The 15 mean-crossings and -12% two-year drift are unchanged, so last year's relative fall still reads as oscillation, not decay. I cut the long and the short in the same proportion so the trim does not quietly convert a spread into a directional semis bet.

Short leg vs TSM, cut from 6.4 to 4.0 against a 5.0 long because KLAC's 2.70 beta still exceeds TSM's 2.15 - beta-matched, not dollar-matched. KLAC closed $183.99 after falling 9.7% on the week, but I trim rather than press because the reason for the fall argues against me: this was a sector-wide de-risking that hit LRCX, AMAT, ASML, MU and AMD alike, and KLAC itself guided fiscal Q1 revenue and profit ABOVE consensus on AI infrastructure demand. Every dollar of the decline was multiple compression, 55.7x to 50.3x, on improving fundamentals. My thesis was that the multiple was the binding constraint; it has now partly given way, so the cheap part of the short has been paid. What holds the residual is that 50x trailing is still an extraordinary price for a cyclical and the target gap versus TSM has not closed to zero, at 6.3 points. This stays my smallest and most violent spread on purpose - a name with a 52-week range of $83 to $307 is the leg most likely to be wrong fastest, which is why it is now the smallest leg in the book.

Long leg vs HD, cut from 11.0 to 6.0 because the specific reason for full size has been consumed and the evidence partly went against me. LOW printed 08-19: adj EPS $4.40 beat $4.22, but revenue of $25.96bn missed $26.16bn, comps rose only +0.2% against HD's +1.7%, and FY guidance was cut to the bottom end - $92bn sales and flat comps versus $92-94bn and flat-to-+2%. That is my long leg guiding down while the leg I am short reaffirmed, which is a fundamental point against the pair, and the pre-print asymmetry I was paid to carry no longer exists. I keep half rather than none because the valuation and target evidence still points my way: LOW at $216.09 sits just above its $199.40 52-week low at 18.3x with a $254.36 target implying 17.7% upside against HD's 12.4%, a 5.3-point gap and a 5.2-turn multiple discount, and total sales still grew 8.3% against HD's 5.7% with online up 15.7%. Hedge quality is second only to WFC/BAC - 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings, -6% two-year drift - and with both prints behind us there is no catalyst inside a full quarter.

Short leg vs LOW, sized 5.7 against 6.0 so the 0.68 and 0.65 betas cancel to within 0.03% of NAV. I state the evidence against this leg plainly: HD cleared the harder bar on 08-18 with sales of $47.9bn up 5.7% versus $47.24bn expected, comps +1.7%, adj EPS $4.92 against $4.73, and full-year guidance held despite the housing slump - all delivered with CEO Ted Decker still on medical leave and the CFO covering, which answers the governance question I raised last week in HD's favour rather than mine. That is why the leg is halved rather than held. What keeps it on is price: at $335.61 HD trades at 23.5x with only 12.4% upside to a $377.50 target, while the demand mix management described is small projects and Pro rather than big discretionary renovation, which is the same soft-DIY backdrop that is being used to mark LOW down five turns cheaper. I carry no stop here, as before: stopping out one side of a beta-matched pair would leave me naked long LOW, and with both companies now a full quarter from their next print, the common housing shock is the only thing left to move them together.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: A calendar-driven book sized off measured Jul-27-to-year-end window statistics computed over 2000-2025 daily history: overweight the sectors with the highest seasonal hit-rates into the Aug-Dec window (industrials, financials, regional banks, large-cap growth), hold gold and utilities as the measured Aug-Sep defensive/flow legs, short the two sleeves that most reliably lag the S&P over the same calendar window (developed non-US equity and intermediate Treasuries), and carry 7% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 seasonal rotations.

positions.thesis: Raised 19% to 20% and my largest leg. The seasonal is unchanged and among my best: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg alone +3.64% in 19/26 years. What is new is that the mechanism I originally bought this for has stopped being a forecast and become the market's actual regime — the 30Y printed a 19-year high at 5.34% and the 10Y a 20-month high at 4.75% on deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and Warsh signalling he will not hike against inflation. Short-end anchored, long-end rising is the steepener that widens net interest margin, and it is now three consecutive weeks old and no longer dependent on the September-hike call that inverted on me twice. The tape confirms independently: XLF ranks 2nd of eleven, sits in the leading RRG quadrant, is holding above its breakout, and carries a 19% weight in the top-five sector model. Credit is cooperative — Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals — and the money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams are the buffer you want owning financials against a 51-print consumer-sentiment reading. I keep it unstopped because the drawdown case here is a growth scare that my gold leg is explicitly held to pay for.

Raised 16% to 18%, funded from XLU, and this is the add I have been waiting a month to make. This remains the strongest statistic in my window set: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone at +4.68%, 81%, t=+3.78 and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. Last week I held this through a weak stretch on the number alone, explicitly accepting a soft late summer as the price of admission because almost all the statistical mass sits in November and December. This week the tape came to the number instead: industrials moved from 6th of eleven to 3rd, took a 12% weight in the top-five model, are heading strongly into the improving quadrant and nearing leadership, and XLI broke out of a multi-month consolidation with positive three-month flows on AI-infrastructure spend, reshoring and defence demand, +16% YTD. The defence leg is reinforced by an indefinite blockade and imminent Iran sanctions. Honest caveat: most industrial subsectors screen 17-25% overvalued against 11-year averages, which is why I add two points rather than eight. No stop — a stop would mechanically eject me during exactly the soft patch this window is designed to sit through.

Held flat at 18% with the +18% take-profit unchanged, and the discipline is the point. Gold rose another 2.39% to $4,680.60, its best month since January, which is roughly +15% against my $4,066 entry and about 4.5x the entire average return of my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54%, 14/21 years, t=+1.69). By strict calendar logic the edge is spent. I still do not cut, for the same reason as last week and a new one. The old reason: selling into a dated, pre-announced catalyst is bad execution, and the Iran stack — stalled Hormuz talks, an indefinite blockade, unprecedented isolation measures — is still live. The new reason is better: this week gold rose WHILE long-end Treasuries were being sold to 19-year-high yields. That is not a rate-cut bid, it is a debasement and Fed-credibility bid, and it is the same Warsh-will-not-hike-against-inflation mechanism that drives my XLF and IEF legs. That makes gold the internally consistent hedge of this book rather than a stray commodity punt. My exit sits near $4,798, about 2.5% away — above anything my seasonal justifies and short of the crowded $5,000-$6,000 sell-side targets, which is the right place to be a seller. No stop: this is the leg that pays if the consumer rollover turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break.

Held flat at 17% with the -15% stop unchanged, and I am deliberately refusing to make this my third directional change on one sleeve in six weeks. The absolute seasonal is what justifies the position and it is intact: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%), on a sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight. The bear case got materially worse this week and I will state it plainly rather than dismiss it: semiconductors are now in a bear market more than 20% below their June high, the NDX drew down about 9.7% from its record, IT shed over 3% in five sessions, and the triggers are real — AVGO's cautious AI-chip guide on top of the $370bn financing-vehicle story I flagged last week, a memory-chip crisis, and China's memory and lithography ambitions. Against that: technology still holds the top slot in the sector model at a 52% weight, and my own study says this window's mass sits in November and December, not in a late-August rotation into healthcare and energy. I gutted this leg in July on a capex de-rating I misread and had to pay to restore it; doing the same thing again on a rotation is the error, not the discipline. The -15% stop is the right instrument for a financing-driven de-rating — it caps the damage without forcing me to pre-judge a debt story that resolves over quarters.

Raised 6% to 8% with the -8% stop unchanged — a half-step, not the 17% I once carried and cut. The seasonal is the most extreme statistic in my study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. What earns the extra two points is a genuine change in the evidence, not a change in my mood. Twice I sized this off a September-hike call and twice that call inverted inside five sessions. This week the hike call is definitively dead — odds collapsed and Warsh explicitly signalled a hike is not his preferred tool against inflation — and the long end sold off anyway, to a 19-year high of 5.34% on the 30Y and a 20-month high of 4.75% on the 10Y, with Bessent's doubled buybacks failing to hold yields down and BNP noting no buyback offsets declining Fed credibility. The surviving mechanism is deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and term premium, which has a much longer half-life than a policy-rate guess, and it is the identical mechanism paying my XLF leg. I stop at 8% for one honest reason: IEF is the 7-10 year belly, the part of the curve a dovish Warsh at his first Jackson Hole next week would rally hardest, and I will not size into a dated catalyst I cannot handicap. The -8% stop stays — a bond rally that large means recession is being priced, and I want out before that correlates with my cyclical longs.

Held flat at 5% with the -18% stop unchanged, and holding is a decision against the obvious argument. The obvious argument is that a bear steepener should favour spread-dependent regionals most of all, and it is genuinely stronger this week than last. I decline it for two reasons. First, the tape still refuses to pay it: the Russell 2000 keeps making records with AI-linked small caps supplying the move while KRE sits well below its 2022 peak — a group that will not rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something the seasonal cannot see. Second, the specific way the curve steepened this week is the wrong way for regionals: 19-year-high long yields mark down available-for-sale securities portfolios, which is the 2023 accident, and regionals lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that cushion the money-centres while CRE nonperformers still rise at select names. So I express the steepener through XLF, which I raised, not here. I keep 5% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured — Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14% — but that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91%. The cheapest way to own the Q4 window is to be small now and rebuild with the Nov-1 rotation cash.

Cut from 9% to 4% — the funding source for XLI, XLF and IEF, and the one leg where my own measured calendar and the live tape finally say the same thing. This is still my largest directional risk and the bear case is unchanged and honest: a deal lands, crude gaps down, and the stop gaps through it. Size is the real protection, which is why 22 and not 30. New take-profit at +40%, roughly a 20% XLE move — around $115-120 Brent, the level where demand destruction, SPR politics and pressure on Tehran to settle invert the risk/reward and I would rather be paid than greedy. Stop held at -22%, capping the leg at ~4.8% of NAV.

Trimmed 25 to 20 to fund MPC and silver, not because it stopped working — it hit 'Confirmed Leader' status on 8/7 and is the second-strongest sector behind energy, at ~18x forward with a 0.65-0.75 beta, carried by real Q2 earnings beats and the GLP-1 franchise rather than by defensive flows. It remains the ballast that makes a 2x energy fund carryable, and 20% is still enough of it to do that job. The honest reason for the trim is that a Fed cutting in September into a weak dollar is a regime where low-beta quality compounds steadily but does not lead, and I found two places this week where the same capital has a sharper edge. No stop, unchanged reasoning: this is the position I want to still own if everything else here is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only fire in a market-wide flush, which is the exact moment I want to be holding it.

Held flat at 20 because this week is what I bought it for and adding after a 5.4% weekly run is chasing. Gold printed ~$4,607 on 8/21, up 2% on the day to a three-month-plus high in record territory, on Powell opening the door to a September cut with markets at 91% odds — while he simultaneously kept inflation risks 'tilted to the upside' with tariff pass-through 'clearly visible.' Cutting into sticky inflation with federal debt through $40 trillion and a soft dollar is the exact monetary setup gold is built for, and it is stacked on a Hormuz premium and central-bank buying, so the bid is layered rather than single-source. It also remains the only asset here that wins in both tails of my own book: stalemate keeps the geopolitical bid alongside ERX, and a sudden settlement that kills ERX lands on a labor market that shed 23,000 jobs and a Fed already cutting. Still bullion rather than GDX — mining operating leverage on top of a 2x energy fund would concentrate variance in the one thing I am trying to reduce. Stop tightened -13% to -12%, capping the leg at 2.4% of NAV: still far outside any headline shakeout, but a 12% break from a record would mean the rate-cut repricing died, and at that point this has stopped hedging.

New 12% position, and the most important change I made. Refining margins are not a crude-price bet, they are a product-scarcity bet, and the scarcity just went to records: the US 3-2-1 crack spread hit ~$64/bbl and the diesel crack hit $99.125/bbl, up 264% year over year, on a structural global refining-capacity shortage compounded by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and reduced fuel exports. MPC's own refining and marketing margin went from $17.58 to $36.33 per barrel and industry margins have nearly tripled since the start of 2026 — that is realized cash, not a forecast. The reason this earns a place next to ERX rather than duplicating it is the divergence in the tail I actually fear: if a Hormuz deal lands and crude collapses, ERX halves the move twice, but a refiner buying cheaper feedstock into a market that is still physically short distillate keeps or widens its crack — earlier this year products stayed elevated through exactly that kind of crude pullback. Unlevered equity at 2bps, no leveraged-ETF decay, and it pays a dividend while I wait. Entering near an all-time-high close ($365.21 on 8/18, $358.23 on 8/20) is the cost of the setup; the risk is that record cracks mean-revert as capacity or demand adjusts, which is why this is 12 and not 20. Stop -18% caps the leg at ~2.2% of NAV.

Held at 10% — both drivers strengthened again and this is the natural pair to a record distillate crack. The cost side is now brutal and confirmed by the industry itself: the global airline sector has nearly HALVED its 2026 profit forecast citing Middle East fuel costs, US carriers' fuel bill ran ~$6.7bn in May at +85% y/y, jet fuel sits in the record-crack complex I just went long via MPC, and carriers are cutting unprofitable routes and grounding less fuel-efficient aircraft — that is management telling you the margin math no longer works. Brent went from $88.52 to $93.86 this week, so the pressure is still increasing, not peaking. The demand side is independent and intact: a contracting labor market with leisure and hospitality specifically soft reads directly on discretionary air travel, and discretionary leisure flinches first as fares rise to cover fuel. Portfolio-wise this is my only equity hedge with the index at records. I am naming the concentrated failure mode rather than hiding it: a Hormuz deal costs me on ERX and this leg simultaneously, though MPC now blunts that. Squeeze risk stays specific — the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a possible government equity stake. Borrow at 3% APR on 10% is ~30bps a year. Stop -18% caps it at 1.8% of NAV; take-profit held at +25%.

Two things make me want more of it here specifically rather than more gold: silver is still meaningfully below its February mid-$80s high while gold is at a record and BTC just posted its best week since 2024, so this is the laggard expression of the debasement trade rather than the chased one; and a Fed easing into 'clearly visible' tariff inflation supports the industrial half of silver demand that a weakening labor market had been cutting against. It stays 10 and not 20 because that industrial component genuinely cuts both ways and because this metal's own history is violent — mid-$80s to $64 to $70 inside a year. Stop stays wide at -18%, capping the leg at 1.8% of NAV; anything tighter is noise on a chart like this.

positions.thesis: Unchanged at 30%, and the one leg where this week was a clean out-of-sample test of last week's correction rather than a new argument. I moved the core from SPY to RSP on the claim that a high-dispersion tape pays the equal-weighted wrapper: RSP then returned -0.49% against SPY's -1.37%, 88bp in five sessions, in exactly the way the thesis predicted - megacap duration got repriced by the long end while the average stock did not. The underlying statistics are unmoved on re-measurement: RSP realizes 11.30% at 20d and 11.23% at 60d against SPY's 13.15% and 14.00%, roughly a fifth less volatility at both horizons, for a matched year of return (+21.24% vs +21.82%) and 71% downside capture across SPY's ten worst sessions. I owe two caveats I will not act on but will not hide either. At 10 days RSP now realizes MORE than SPY, 10.18% against 7.85%, because the volatility has rotated out of megacap tech - XLK's rv10 of 17.59 is half its rv20 of 32.42 - and into the energy, materials and healthcare names that equal-weight overweights; and RSP's beta to 30y yield changes is worse than SPY's at 60d, -0.91 against -0.57, so if the term-premium shock is the dominant driver from here the equal-weight tilt is not the hedge, it is a mild liability. Both are single-window readings against 20-day, 60-day and one-year evidence pointing the other way, and I said last week I refuse to trade on ten days of realized vol alone, so I hold. The -14% stop stays a regime brake rather than a trading stop, set to the same ~1.3 annual sigma severity as SPY's -18% given RSP's lower realized vol, so the two core legs stop at equivalent pain rather than at equivalent-looking numbers.

Trimmed from 20% to 14%, and the reason is a change in what I know rather than a change in how I feel. Last week I kept 20% on the explicit grounds that I had volatility data but no leadership forecast, so a full exit would be a conviction bet on equal-weight leadership I had not earned. I now have a mechanism instead of a forecast: the 30-year Treasury printed 5.31-5.33% this week, a 19-year high, driven by a $1.9T deficit, heavy long-end supply and five years of above-target inflation - a term-premium move, with ^IRX pinned at 3.71 while ^TNX rose to 4.74. A term-premium shock is a discount-rate shock, and discount-rate shocks are duration-selective: they hit the longest-dated cash flows hardest. That is not a style preference, it is arithmetic, and the tape obeyed it - XLK -3.53%, SMH -4.66%, Meta ~-7% in a week SPY lost 1.37% and the equal-weighted index lost 0.49%. SPY's ~40% megacap concentration is the most duration-extended block of equity I own, so it is the correct place to fund a hedge against the risk that is actually running. I am trimming rather than eliminating because the argument is still relative and the counter-evidence is real: SPY realizes only 7.85% at 10 days, it returned +21.82% over the year, its 60d yield beta (-0.57) is actually better than RSP's (-0.91), and Bessent's surprise Treasury buyback on 08-19 already pulled the 30y back to 5.276 for a net +1bp week - the shock is being leaned against, and a Fed or Treasury that succeeds in capping the long end hands leadership straight back to duration. Keeping 14% means being wrong about that costs me a slice rather than the position. The -18% stop stays wide and deliberately loose: XLE, COMT and VIXY are the actual hedges in this book, and stacking a tight stop on top of paid-for convexity double-buys the same insurance and invites a whipsaw exit at the worst possible moment.

Unchanged at 18%, and after this week's testing it is the leg I would defend hardest. I went looking for a reason to cut it, because min-vol portfolios are structurally heavy in staples, utilities and healthcare - classic bond proxies - and a long-end shock is exactly where that composition should have hurt. It did not: USMV printed +0.10% in a week SPY lost 1.37% and XLU lost 3.48%, and its measured beta to 30y yield changes is -0.40 at 60d and -0.32 at 1y, the smallest magnitude of any equity sleeve in my book against RSP's -0.91, SPY's -0.57 and XLU's -0.45. MSCI's optimizer excludes high-volatility constituents outright, so the ~32% technology label sits in low-beta software, services and payments rather than in the semiconductor complex realizing 45%, and the same screen keeps it out of the most rate-levered utilities. It realizes 8.76% at 20d, the lowest of anything I own, captured roughly 37% of SPY's move across the year's ten worst sessions, and is +4.85% over the past month against SPY's +2.33%. The honest cost is the one I glossed last week: over a full year USMV returned +8.96% against SPY's +21.82%, so this is genuinely a regime-conditional sleeve and not a free lunch - it is a drag whenever beta is being paid, and it is being paid nothing right now. Its role is precise and unchanged: it is the only thing I own that keeps working in a soft-landing rotation that punishes beta without producing a volatility event or an inflation shock, which is the single state where the equity core, the commodity hedge and VIXY all fail together. Stop unchanged at -14%, capping the leg near -2.5% of NAV.

Raised from 7% to 9%, but the reason for owning it has changed from the one I wrote last week and that matters more than the size. I bought it as a generic decorrelated crash hedge that happened to fit an inflation story. I have now measured what it actually does against the specific risk that is live: regressed on daily 30-year yield changes, XLE's beta is +1.86%/10bp at 60d and +1.40 at 1y, and across the twelve largest yield-up days of the trailing year it printed positive on eight with an average of +0.72%. It is the only long leg in my entire universe with a positive sign there - SPY -0.57, RSP -0.91, USMV -0.40, XLU -0.45, TLT -1.56. So this is not a decorrelator I hope will help, it is the one instrument that is measurably paid by the thing that hurts everything else I own, and it still holds up on the original test too: positive on five of SPY's ten worst sessions, average -0.10% against SPY's -1.87%, 60d beta to SPY of -0.52. The fundamental case escalated rather than resolved. Brent is ~$94 after a second consecutive ~6% week, roughly +13% in two, on Hormuz transits still severely constrained with Middle East production shut in and Ukrainian strikes taking out Russian refining, and Bessent announces new Iran isolation measures Monday 08-24. That impulse is also the mechanism feeding the September hike risk, which makes this leg a hedge against the Fed leg of the same trade. I am adding only 2% rather than loading the whole hedge here for two disciplined reasons: a position already +8.79% on the month deserves respect rather than enthusiasm, and roughly 15% of XLE is refiners whose crack spreads can compress on precisely a transit-disruption shock, while XOM and CVX alone are 35% of the fund. The rest of the hedge goes to COMT, which carries neither wedge. The -22% stop is intentionally tighter in sigma terms (~0.9 annual sigma at 25% realized) than my core legs, because this is a thematic position with a binary geopolitical driver and a de-escalation headline is a real path; it caps the leg near -2.0% of NAV.

New, and it exists to hold the half of the inflation hedge that XLE cannot cleanly express. XLE is equity in producers and refiners; COMT is direct exposure to the commodity complex itself via a dynamic-roll GSCI strategy, so it has no crack-spread wedge - refiners can lose on exactly the transit-disruption shock I am hedging, because input costs move before product prices - and no single-name concentration against XOM and CVX at 35% of XLE. The numbers justify it on its own terms and not just as diversification: beta to 30y yield changes +1.34%/10bp at 60d (versus SPY -0.57 and RSP -0.91), positive on seven of the twelve largest yield-up days, +0.04% average across SPY's ten worst sessions with five of ten positive, 60d beta to SPY of -0.41 - the most negative equity correlation of any candidate I screened - and +43.5% over the trailing year, so the protection is not bought with surrendered return. I chose it over DBC and PDBC deliberately: all three carry near-identical yield beta (+1.67, +1.71, +1.34), but COMT realizes 18.9% at 20d against DBC's 26.5%, which is roughly 90% of the hedge for 71% of the volatility, and its broader basket beyond energy meant it actually led the complex this week at +4.11% against XLE's +2.79%. Backtesting the split against loading the full 15% into either instrument alone: XLE-only raises book volatility to 5.34%, COMT-only deepens max drawdown to -2.66%, and the blend lands at 5.03% and -2.34% - the diversification is measurable, not cosmetic. Sized at 6% with a -20% stop, tighter in sigma terms than my core legs for the same reason as XLE: the driver is a geopolitical binary that can reverse on a headline, and the two commodity legs together are capped at roughly -3.2% of NAV.

Held at 7%, and I want the record to show I intended to raise it and the evidence stopped me. Two findings argued for adding. First, VVIX printed 86.27, the 2nd percentile of two years - options on VIX itself are the cheapest they have been in my entire sample, which is the purest read on how little convexity costs. Second, I had measured the premium against the wrong window: last week I compared VIX to 10-day realized (7.28 points, 63rd percentile) and called it normal, but VIX is a 30-day forward measure and the tenor-matched comparison is VIX minus rv20, which is 1.98 points at the 27th percentile against a 4.11 two-year mean. Implied vol is cheap, not rich, and that reverses my conclusion. Two dated binaries sit inside the horizon: Warsh's debut Jackson Hole keynote on 08-28, from a chair who has abolished forward guidance, and a 09-16 FOMC now priced ~1-in-3 for a HIKE with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan already having dissented for one - a hike risk, which is the opposite of what I assumed last week. And the carry objection I cut on has largely dissolved: beta-adjusted excess drag was -7.63%/week over the last five sessions but +0.05%/week over 21 days, so the ~50% annualised figure I acted on was a spike, not a level. Then I tested the sizing before trading it, and the test came back against me. Across the trailing year the book returns +14.02% at 7% VIXY, +11.81% at 9% and +10.46% at 11%, with max drawdown deepening from -2.34% to -2.67% and the ten-worst-day average improving only from -0.25% to +0.05% - over a year containing ten sessions worse than -1.5%, every marginal point above 7% cost more carry than it recovered, and it also crushed upside participation, cutting the ten-best-day average from +0.26% to +0.04%. Cheap convexity and convexity worth buying are different claims. I also tested swapping into VIXM and rejected it: VIXM delivers 1.92% on SPY's worst days against VIXY's 7.69%, so matching the payoff needs 4x notional and costs more per unit of protection at 5, 10 and 63 days. So the leg stays exactly as it is, at a size that is honestly a tail hedge rather than a position. Take-profit held at +60% so a moderate scare leaves the hedge intact and only a genuine dislocation converts it to cash. No stop, for the reason that never changes: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.
