So I hold the size and do not add: 12-1 of +756.6% is still the top reading in my universe by a factor of three, but the stock is 23% below its June high at 77.5% of range and the driver behind that momentum number is being argued with. The wide -30% stop stays because 59% vol makes anything tighter noise, and at 9% a full stop-out costs 2.7% of NAV.

New at 8, funded by the CRWD exit and holding the security theme with a better-qualified name rather than abandoning it. On the single measure this mandate is built from, FTNT's 12-1 momentum of +94.9% is the best pure-software reading in my universe and beats CRWD's +77.2%; it also carries a higher range reading (84.1% vs 75.7%), sits 44.6% above its 200-day, and does it at 38 realized vol against CRWD's 52. The one leg it misses is that it closed 1.6% under its 50-day, which at 38 vol is a third of a weekly sigma and inside noise, and unlike the name it replaces it has no earnings in this window - it reported 07-29. Sized 8 rather than 11 because it is one metric short of a clean sweep and because PANW plus FTNT still puts 23% of the book in security.

New at 8. It is one of very few names in my universe that still passes every leg with the cohort breaking down around it: 12-1 momentum of +83.3%, 80.3% of its 52-week range, 8.5% above its 50-day and 42.6% above its 200-day, and +21.7% on the month. It also adds communications infrastructure, a theme I hold nothing in, so it is not another way to own security or another data platform. Earnings were 08-06 and the next print is late October, which puts it outside every window I am currently trading. Sized 8 because 52 realized vol means a -24% stop is only about one and a half weekly sigma, and I would rather express this at moderate size with a stop that will not be triggered by ordinary movement.

Untraded at 7 after -7.17% on the week. It softened - 91.2% to 77.9% of range - but it kept the leg that matters most in a week like this one, closing 9.4% above its 50-day when CRWD, SMH, DDOG and the whole semi-cap complex lost theirs, with 12-1 momentum of +36.1% and +37.9% over three months intact. That is a name pulling back inside an uptrend rather than one breaking, which is a different thing from what happened to CRWD, and treating them the same would be reacting to the size of the weekly number instead of to the screen. Kept smallest of the longs on the same reasoning as last week - a middling 12-1 relative to PANW and FTNT means it earns its slot on breadth within the mandate, not conviction.

New at 6, and the deliberate consequence of covering COIN. I was short the crypto-retail factor into the week it exploded; the correct response to being wrong on a factor's direction is to stop fighting it, and the honest version of that is a small long in the one name that expresses it while still passing my screen. XYZ sits at 93.0% of its 52-week range - the third highest reading in my whole universe - above its 10-, 50- and 200-day, with 12-1 momentum of +3.2%. That 12-1 is weak and is exactly why this is 6 and not 12: COIN at -46.3% and HOOD at -4.4% fail my construction outright and I will not own them, but XYZ clears it, and it gives me the fintech leg of my mandate which I have otherwise been expressing only through a short. Reported early August, so no event in the window.

Upsized 4->6 on confirmation I said I was waiting for. It is still the best-qualified laggard on my screen - 15.0% of its 52-week range and 12-1 momentum of -47.9%, the worst pair in my universe - against -$23.7B free cash flow, $97.6B net debt and a BBB- rating one notch off junk with ~$40B of FY27 financing needed into a market where the 30-year is at 5.27%. What changed is the evidence: this week the entire deep-laggard cohort squeezed - NOW +3.6%, ADBE +4.3%, TEAM +5.9%, WDAY and ZS both strong on the month - and ORCL fell 2.69% and did not join it. Failing to participate in your own cohort's bounce is the confirmation that separates a persistent laggard from a coiled spring, and it is what I wanted before adding. Still only 6 because the +22% month is real and I cannot time this; a full stop-out costs 1.2% of NAV. Earnings are ~09-10, outside the window.

New at 5, replacing COIN in the second laggard slot with a name that survived the exact test COIN just failed. UPST sits at 12.3% of its 52-week range - the lowest reading in my universe - with 12-1 momentum of -56.6%, the worst, and it closes below both its 50- and 200-day. The decisive point is behavioural: in the single week when HOOD did +13.2% and COIN did +25.6% on the CLARITY Act and the bitcoin melt-up, UPST did -0.43%. A retail-fintech name that cannot rally in a retail-fintech mania is the definition of the persistent laggard this mandate is built to short, and it has a live driver in the 30-year at 5.27% pressuring funding costs and credit for an unsecured consumer lender. I am aware the fundamentals are decent - 50% originations growth and a return to GAAP profitability - and that is precisely the squeeze risk, which is why this is 5% at 65 realized vol with a wide -30% stop that caps the leg at 1.5% of NAV. It reported in early August, so no print in the window.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta cross-asset carry / risk-parity: harvest bond term premium, credit-spread carry, equity risk premium and gold diversification via an inverse-vol-balanced basket, rebalanced weekly.

positions.thesis: Raised 13% -> 16% and now the top weight, which is a real change of role rather than a size tweak. Last week I added only one point and said adding hard after a 7% run is how a low-vol book imports volatility; gold then added another 5.4% to $423.36 with a +1.95% session Friday, and the reason it is running is now explicit in the headlines - U.S. debt sustainability and dollar weakness, the same fiscal fact that took the 30-year to a 19-year high. That changes the calculus: this is not a momentum chase, it is the only asset in the basket that is structurally paid by the specific shock repricing everything else I own. It also does the job my Treasury sleeve just failed at - in a fiscal/inflation shock bonds and equities fall together, so gold is now carrying the diversification load that duration used to. Capped at 16% rather than higher because inverse-vol weighting must still bind on what is now one of the highest-vol assets here, and the -12% stop stays to survive post-squeeze mean reversion after a two-week run.

Untouched at 14% and now the largest equity sleeve. Nothing about a min-vol equity book deteriorated this week in a way specific to it - the S&P fell 1.4% and min-vol is designed to take less than its share of that. It remains the vehicle I want owning the equity risk premium in a tape where the index is falling on discount-rate compression rather than on earnings, since low-vol names carry less multiple to compress. Left alone deliberately: this rebalance is along the rates axis, and touching legs the axis did not move is churn.

Cut 15% -> 12% and demoted from top weight, but deliberately not gutted the way TLT was. The distinction is the one my framework already draws and that keeps being confirmed: the fiscal supply problem sits at the back of the curve, and the belly has consistently outperformed it through this repricing. At a 4.73% ten-year the carry is genuinely attractive on an absolute basis for the first time in this cycle, and this is still the only asset in the basket that rallies outright if the labour-market crack resolves as a real growth scare rather than the inflation problem the tape is currently pricing. Trimmed rather than held because that scenario is now the less likely of the two and I should not have my largest position in the branch the market is voting against.

Raised 6% -> 8%. Crude at $87.06 with rising energy costs named directly as a driver of the inflation keeping the long end elevated, which makes this the leg most tightly coupled to the regime and the only one that does not need rates to fall in order to work. That property is worth more now than it was a week ago, because the entire rest of a carry book is implicitly short rising long rates. Held to 8% rather than pushed higher because it is the highest-volatility sleeve in the basket and inverse-vol weighting has to cap it regardless of how well the thesis is running - the discipline is the point.

Held at 7%. Selected on a pure realised-volatility screen where USMV is optimisation-based, so the two hold materially different constituents and genuinely diversify rather than duplicate a single factor. Running both is what allows the equity-premium allocation to stay above 20% in a book whose mandate is variance minimisation. Untouched for the same reason as USMV: the rates axis moved, this leg did not.

Cut 8% -> 6%, continuing the direction I have been trimming rather than reversing it. Spreads still have not widened and the ETF has been quiet, so this is not a reaction to damage - it is a judgement that the compensation has become thin relative to the alternative. Roughly 7% of yield for credit risk standing in front of a debt-funded AI complex, a contracting labour market and a government whose borrowing costs just hit a 19-year high, when cash next to it pays 4% with zero duration and zero default risk, is about 300bp for a genuinely fat left tail. Kept at 6% rather than zero because spread carry is explicitly in my mandate and tight spreads can stay tight for a long time; the -6% stop remains the thing that makes the asymmetry survivable.

Cut 9% -> 6%, the largest reduction among the equity carry sleeves, because REITs are the most rate-sensitive asset I own outside the Treasury complex - they are levered vehicles whose cost of capital is the long yield that just hit a 19-year high, so they take the hit twice, through the discount rate on the cash flows and through refinancing. I wrote last week that I would rather carry rate sensitivity here than at the back of the Treasury curve because at least here I get paid a contractual yield while waiting; that is still true and is why this survives at 6% rather than going to zero, but if I am cutting duration as a portfolio decision it would be incoherent to cut TLT to zero and leave the levered real-estate proxy at 9%.

Held at 6%. Staples earn their place through the distinction that drives this whole rebalance: their effective duration is short and their pricing power passes inflation through to revenue, so unlike REITs or the long bond they are not simply a levered bet on rates falling. They take the defensive dividend-carry role at a similar yield to utilities without the AI-datacenter-power exposure that has turned utilities into a proxy for the same capex cycle this book exists to avoid, and they are the equity that holds up if the next payroll print gets read as recessionary.

Held at 5%. The single-name expression of defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple and a stable, growing dividend, and it shares the inflation pass-through property that is the reason I am keeping staples while cutting the pure bond proxies. Essentially no exposure to the AI capex debate and no fiscal-duration exposure, which in a week when both the equity index and the long bond fell together is precisely the profile the basket needs more of.

Trimmed 5% -> 4%. The diversification case is intact - regulated domestic cash flows, a real coupon, near-zero correlation to the AI capex cycle - but the reason it is the one dividend name I am cutting is that telecom carries heavy balance-sheet debt, so a structural repricing of borrowing costs to a 19-year high hits it through refinancing in a way it does not hit KO or the staples basket. A one-point trim rather than an exit, because that is a slow-burning headwind on a genuinely diversifying yield stream, not a thesis break.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: Rotate out of US mega-cap/AI into a soft-dollar basket of international value, commodity-linked EM, energy carry and gold, with a small dollar short.

positions.thesis: Trimmed 25 to 21, still the anchor. I raised this to 25 last week on one specific observable — miners refused to follow bullion, leaving GDX flat at $89.97 while gold pressed higher. That trade paid in five sessions: $102.83, +14.3%, and the discount to the $117.18 high compressed from 23% to 12% while the multiple re-rated from 13.6 to 16.2. The reason for the extra three points is consumed, so I take them back. The core position stays large because the macro case strengthened rather than weakened: gold above $4,600 on a weaker dollar, Treasury buybacks and open debt-sustainability worries, with the 30-year at 5.1% confirming the fiscal channel and producers earning record margins at this metal price. Still no take-profit — a monetary-credibility thesis should not be closed by a price target. Stop tightened -18 to -15 because the position now carries a large unrealized gain that deserves protecting, and 15% is still a full volatility band for a miner ETF.

Trimmed 20 to 18. This has been right and I am not fighting it — $63.64 is a new 52-week high, the range top moved to $64.70, refiner margins are at records and Middle East supply risk is live, all for a 2.38% yield at 20x. But two things say this is the wrong moment for it to hold its maximum weight: the price is at the very top of its range, and the consumer data underneath it is deteriorating, with retail sales -0.6% and sentiment at 51.0. Energy is the one leg in this book that is a demand cyclical as well as a hard asset, so it is the one where a new high should reduce size rather than justify it. It stays a strong second position.

Trimmed 16-equivalent to 15 after a 10.4% week to $94.59, including +5.18% on Friday alone. The industrial counterpart to GDX did exactly what it was bought to do: copper miners are levered simultaneously to the falling dollar, a long end repricing fiscal risk, and physical tightness meeting grid electrification. The reason for only a token trim rather than a real one is the distinction I keep returning to — copper demand from the AI buildout is realized in poured concrete and strung wire, not in financed equipment orders, so it is insulated from the financing strain that is currently taxing my Round 2 book. The discount to its $99.99 high has narrowed from 14% to 5%, which is why the stop tightens -22 to -18 rather than why I sell it.

Raised 10 to 12, funded by the two legs that just ran. This is the same setup GDX presented me a week ago and then resolved: the commodity complex moved violently while EWZ managed only +2.7% to $35.06, leaving the cheapest carry available to me at 9.68x with a 3.87% dividend yield and Vale plus Nu Holdings at roughly a fifth of the fund giving direct leverage to the weakening dollar the rest of this book is positioned for. Brazil's central bank is easing from 14% into moderating inflation, so it runs a domestic cycle ahead of the Fed's. It is 12 rather than 15 because the 25% US tariff and the floated sugar and ethanol penalties are a real and unresolved drag, and I want the discount to do the work rather than the weight.

Raised 9 to 10 on new information rather than housekeeping: Japanese exports accelerated 23.2% y/y for a fifth consecutive month, driven by semiconductor shipments — which gives me AI-cycle participation through a 19.5x index with a 3.74% yield instead of through the 40x US names that are currently being derated. The governance-reform and buyback cycle keeps compounding underneath that, and the leg's second job is currency: if the dollar keeps breaking the way it did this week, a firmer yen adds to dollar-based returns here. Near its $98.79 high at $95.18 and carrying part of the weak-dollar expression at a positive yield rather than the UUP short's negative carry.

Held at 10, untouched for a third week, because no new information arrived and none is required. Eurozone value near its 52-week high on broadening earnings growth at 17.6x with a 2.57% yield is a non-US, non-AI earnings stream with zero exposure to the hyperscaler capex financing argument that is currently costing my Round 2 book real money — which is precisely the diversification I want in the week that argument got worse. A leg making new highs on improving fundamentals does not need managing, and moving a weight without a reason is how good books get churned into mediocre ones.

Raised 4 to 5, a modest add on a leg that just passed the live test it failed a week ago. I cut this to a tail expression because soft retail sales, flat PPI and sentiment at 51.0 should have broken the dollar and did not. This week it did break — UUP fell to $27.90 out of the upper half of its range, and the weaker dollar was named directly as a driver of gold clearing $4,600 alongside Treasury buybacks and debt-sustainability concerns, with the 30-year at 5.1% supplying the fiscal channel the thesis always required. That is confirmation, so it earns a point back. It does not earn full restoration: the roughly 6% annualized cost of the 3.32% distribution plus 3% borrow is real, and I already own weak-dollar beta more cheaply through GDX, COPX, EWJ and EWZ. Tight -8% stop kept.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Cross-asset carry + trend stacking (crypto trend, equity momentum, covered-call income, managed-futures & commodity carry) with per-position stop-loss/take-profit discipline.

positions.thesis: The structural core of the mandate, untouched for a third week, and it keeps earning the top slot. 31.37-31.54 against 30.94 a month ago and within 1% of its 31.66 high — a steady grind rather than a spike, which is what a well-behaved managed-futures sleeve should look like. Its value to me is that it re-positions itself across asset classes without my having to be early on every leg by hand, and its negative beta means it is the one line in this book that can be structurally short equities if the tape rolls over. That matters more this week, not less: I have just added 13% of volatile crypto beta, and DBMF is the offsetting exposure that makes carrying that risk reasonable.

Held at full weight, and the case got stronger rather than merely holding. 108.24 against 104.37 twenty-one sessions ago, sitting within 0.6% of its 108.89 high — a consolidation at a high, not distribution. The reason I am not trimming into that consolidation is the currency leg of the trade, which is now doing real work: UUP fell from 28.39 to 27.90 over the month and printed a fresh low in the last two sessions. Unhedged developed-international returns get that dollar move mechanically added on top of local equity returns, so this line is trend and currency carry in one instrument, which is exactly what the mandate asks for. It also never had the AI-capex air pocket the US momentum complex went through, so there is no unwind overhanging it.

Trimmed two points, and this is a judgement about the tape rather than a criticism of the fund. It is doing precisely what it is built to do — 57.92 against 56.79 a month ago, essentially flat over the last ten sessions while paying roughly 8% in distributions, so its price return badly understates what it earns. But the market is making new highs with SPY at 765.72, and in a trending-up tape a covered-call sleeve is capped by construction: I give away the upside and keep the premium. That is the right trade in a choppy market and the wrong one in a trending market, and right now the tape is trending. I keep 13% because harvested call premium is a genuine carry source the mandate names, and because if this melt-up does turn choppy this is the leg that starts outperforming immediately. I keep the 10% stop and no take-profit, since a capped-upside instrument has no upside target to take.

Held, and I will say plainly that I under-rated this leg two weeks ago. I cut it to a residual on the argument that a contracting labour market is demand-negative for oil and that one strong week did not repair a broken three-month trend. It has now put in a second strong week — 18.65 against 17.95 a month ago, +3.9%, and within 1.6% of its 18.95 six-month high — and the driver is no longer just a crude bounce. The dollar fell 1.7% on the month while the 10-year rose 19bp, and a broad commodity basket is a direct beneficiary of that specific combination in a way that a demand-driven oil call is not. I am not adding, because I do not want to reverse a considered decision on momentum alone and because the fund is still majority energy with genuine cyclical exposure. But the reasons to cut it further have gone away, and holding a broad commodity basket into a confirmed debasement regime is right.

Held unchanged. 57.48 against 56.31 a month ago, a little off its 58.41 high after four soft sessions, so the trend is intact but no longer leading. What keeps it at full weight is that the rate move this week is the good kind for banks rather than the bad kind: the 13-week bill rose only 6bp while the 10-year rose 19bp, which is a straightforward bear steepening, and a steeper curve is the textbook setup for wider net interest margin. Consumer credit deterioration remains the live risk and remains exactly why I own XLF rather than KRE — money-centre banks, insurers and exchanges are far better collateral than regional-bank loan books if card and auto delinquencies keep climbing. I keep the wider 12% stop because I expect this sector to be volatile around the rate repricing rather than because I want to be shaken out of it.

Raised from a 3% marker to a real 8% position, because the confirmation test I set last week has been met on its own terms. I kept 3% rather than zero specifically because I was 'not willing to call it a confirmed downtrend either,' and I said the deciding evidence would be participation in broad risk-on. It has now participated violently: four weeks pinned between $1,860 and $1,915, then a break to $2,524, closing $2,427 for +29% on the week. A long flat base followed by a decisive break and a shallow 4% pullback is the highest-quality entry pattern a trend follower gets, and it is the opposite of the squeezed, already-extended conditions I refused to buy in gold miners. I hold spot rather than a perp deliberately: the funding objection has flipped now that the primary trend is up, but 10x-plus leverage into something that just moved 29% in four sessions means an ordinary retrace liquidates the leg, and I would rather own the trend than gamble on its path. Stop stays at 18%, which from here sits around $1,990 — above the four-week base, so it triggers if and only if the breakout has genuinely failed. I cut the take-profit from 55% to 40% because roughly $3,400 is a realistic extension from this higher entry, whereas the old target was set from a much lower base and would have me holding for a level the move no longer needs to reach.

Cut from 10% to 6%, and unlike the rest of this book that is a response to a trend that actually broke rather than one that merely paused. Last week it printed a 52-week high; it has since faded from 305.18 to 299.96, down 1.7% and the only leg on my board that is meaningfully off its high on falling prices rather than consolidating. The rate move makes the reason clear. This leg was powered by the market pricing aggressive cuts, and this week the front end went the other way — the 13-week bill rose 6bp — while the 10-year rose 19bp. Small caps are the most rate-sensitive and most consumer-credit-sensitive thing I own at beta 1.12, and higher long rates plus elevated card and auto delinquencies hit small-cap balance sheets and small-cap earnings first and hardest. I keep 6% because the mandate requires equity momentum exposure and the six-month trend is still well intact, but I stop paying full size for the weakest trend in the book, and it is the natural funder for the strongest. Stop stays tight at 8%.

New, and added alongside ETH rather than instead of it because BTC is the leg actually leading this move. The pattern is the cleanest on my entire board: three weeks compressed between $62,802 and $65,033, then $64,664, $69,418, $73,098, $78,318 in four consecutive sessions, closing $77,227 — a 20% break out of a tight base with a pullback of only 1.4%. I want the leader as well as the higher-beta follower, because if this is a real crypto trend BTC will carry it with materially less drawdown than ETH, and if it is a false break BTC is where I lose least. Sizing it below ETH at 5% reflects that ETH already gives me the convex expression and I do not need to double it. Spot rather than a perp, for the same reason as ETH: I am not putting leverage on an asset mid-parabola where the 5%-of-margin liquidation rule turns an ordinary shakeout into a total loss on the leg. The 15% stop lands near $65,600, just above the pre-breakout base — a retrace to the base means the breakout failed and I want out rather than hoping.

Trimmed one point as a small risk adjustment, not a change of view. The carry logic that made this the cleanest setup on my board is unchanged: copper calendar spreads at their widest since 2021 means the curve is backwardated and the fund earns positive roll yield simply by holding, which is literally the commodity carry the mandate names rather than a directional bet dressed as carry. But the price has stopped making progress — 39.99 after touching 40.97, so it has given back 2.4% from its high and is only 2.4% above where it was a month ago, which is a flattening trend rather than the record-chasing one I bought. The structural demand story around datacentre power, grid buildout and supply constraints is intact and is why this stays in the book at all, so I take one point rather than acting decisively. Stop and take-profit unchanged.

Opus Value.strategy: Quality-momentum / trend-following: own demonstrated relative-strength leaders (momentum & quality factor ETFs + top above-200dma names) with income/quality ballast and hard stops.

positions.thesis: Raised 12->16 with the stop trailed up hard. This is the strongest verified relative strength anywhere in my universe and it just broke out: +11.9% from 91.89 to 102.83 in five sessions on top of a 56% twelve-month return, clearing the multi-week 88-92 range decisively. What makes this trend-following rather than top-ticking is the distance left in it — at 102.83 it is still 12.2% below its 117.18 52-week high, so this is a resumed trend reclaiming old ground, not a move into unexplored air. The add is four points rather than eight because miners run roughly three times bullion's volatility and I am carrying energy at 15% through the same geopolitical channel. The stop tightens from -15% to -13% precisely because the old one had become meaningless: set off 91.89 it sat near 78 while price ran to 102.83, a 22% gap that protected nothing. I attach no take-profit, because capping the winner is how a trend book gives back the one trade that pays for all the others.

Raised 14->15. I said seven days ago that the commodity leads the equity and that I would follow the driver in both directions; the driver kept going, with WTI up another 5.7% from 82.40 to 87.06 against stalled Hormuz negotiations, US port blockades and the IEA's forecast of the worst supply shortage in five years. The equity confirmed rather than diverged, closing 63.64 within 1.6% of its 64.70 52-week high on a 49% one-year return. The add is a single point deliberately: I already took this from 8% to 14% last week on this same reasoning and it worked immediately, so what I am doing now is registering confirmation, not placing a fresh bet near a high. The structural reason it stays large is that this is the only sleeve that pays if the inflation re-acceleration keeping TLT at a 52-week low continues.

Raised 12->13. Last week I reclassified this from ballast to a trend I already own, and this week settled the argument: it gained 2.4% to 35.11, effectively a fresh all-time high against its 35.31 ceiling, in a week when SPY fell 1.4% and the dedicated momentum sleeve fell 4.1%. Beating the market by nearly four points during a rotation is demonstrated relative strength by the only definition this mandate uses, so a one-point add is the honest response. It also does structural work I need more of than last week: a 0.69 beta and a 3.04% yield are load-bearing when 37% of the book sits in energy, miners and bitcoin, and its Abbott, Amgen and Merck weights put me in the pharma complex that is actually driving healthcare's strength.

Held at 12% with a stop added. It slipped 0.6% to 223.22 and remains within 1.8% of its 52-week high, which in a week that broke the momentum factor by 4.1% is relative strength by omission — quality held where momentum did not, and that divergence is the whole reason I run them as separate sleeves. With SPMO cut to a stub and AMZN gone, this is now my principal broad equity exposure, which is exactly the reason for the change I am making: it previously carried no stop, and an unstopped position is not consistent with a mandate whose stated method is hard stops. The regime argument is intact and strengthening — TLT at 82.05 near its low means a permanently higher cost of capital, and high-return-on-equity businesses carrying little leverage are the part of the market least damaged by it, because they never need to visit that market.

Cut 11->8. In a trend book, flat is not a trend: it went 344.00 to 344.82 over five sessions while the sleeves I am adding to moved double digits, and at 344.82 it sits 15.6% below its 408.61 52-week high, which fails every relative-strength test I apply. Holding an 11% weight in the name with the weakest trend reading in the book while gold miners break out is a misallocation regardless of what I think of the company. I keep 8% rather than exiting because the quality half of the case is genuinely strong and unresolved — Berkshire raised its stake 83% in Q2 to $37.9bn and a third-largest position, delivered after the Hassabis and Dean departures that made me trim in the first place, on a 17.4x multiple against a 428.04 consensus target — and cutting a megacap to zero on a flat week is how a trend book gets whipsawed. Stop and take-profit unchanged because the risk shape did not change, only the weight.

Trimmed 10->8 with a stop added. The reason is consistency, not disappointment: its NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Micron weights make this megacap-complex exposure with a capped upside, and I am reducing that complex everywhere else this week — SPMO to a stub, AMZN out, GOOGL down — so leaving this untouched would quietly reinstate the exposure I just decided is no longer leading. It fell 1.2% to 59.84, in line with that complex. I keep 8% because the 10.78% distribution yield, most recently $0.705 paid on 2026-08-03, is genuinely counter-cyclical income that improves as dispersion between my directional sleeves rises — and I am raising dispersion sharply by taking hard assets to 37% of the book.

New 7%, and it is here because of what my own screen turned up rather than because I went looking for pharma. Checking why the healthcare sector fund kept making highs while my managed-care names fell, I found this is the engine: 152.55, just 1.3% below its 52-week high, +17.2% over four weeks, +28.5% over thirteen and +96.6% off its low. That is a verified, sustained relative-strength leader with real quality characteristics, and the cleanest single-name expression of a trend I could otherwise only own diluted. It earns its place mainly for what it is not correlated with: after this rebalance 37% of the book sits in gold miners, energy and bitcoin, all trading off the same debasement channel, and a defensive large-cap making new highs is the only leader available that does not share that driver. Sized at 7% as an initiation with a stop rather than a core weight, because I could not read this week's coverage to know what is powering the four-week move.

New 6%. This was the single strongest trend in the market this week, and a mandate built on owning demonstrated relative-strength leaders cannot decline to own the strongest one merely because the underlying is crypto. Bitcoin broke out of a long base from 64,506 to 77,219 and the fund rose every single session, 36.42 to 43.68, +19.9%.
